title: Stand and fight Calum Stuart
content:
Credit: Ivan Weiss The day I interviewed Daniel York Loh, there was news of anti-immigration protests—some of which turned violent—erupting across Belfast, Northern Ireland. The BBC reported that people had been targeted simply for having “a different skin colour”.

In recent years, xenophobic and racist rhetoric has been on the rise in the UK. This has manifested alongside right-wing politicians and political parties (such as Nigel Farage, leader of Reform UK, and Tommy Robinson, a far-right activist) moving from fringe entities into mainstream influence. For Loh—an actor, writer, and filmmaker of Singaporean and British heritage who has been a vocal supporter of left-wing causes—these developments have been equal parts alarming and maddening.

Based in London, Loh has been working in the performing arts in both the UK and Asia for more than forty years. In that time, he’s become increasingly invested in working to improve Asian representation on stage and on screen. He was a founding member of BEATS (British East and Southeast Asian in Theatre and on Screen), a not-for-profit, volunteer-based advocacy group for British East and Southeast Asians working in theatre, film, or television. author: Mekong Review 2
title: No one owes you a living Kirsten Han
content:
Singapore declares itself a “pro-family” country, but there’s a gap between ideal and reality. Credit: Singapore Stock Photos / Unsplash Unease: Life in Singapore Families Teo You Yenn Ethos Books: 2026 . On the surface, Singapore gleams. It’s wealthy, orderly, safe. The trains (generally) run on time, the amenities are plentiful, and the tiny city-state punches above its weight in international rankings to do with governance and education. Singapore is regularly brought up by policy wonks and politicians around the world—and across the political spectrum—as a model to learn from. The government enthusiastically proclaims itself to be “pro-family”, gearing policies towards supporting (heterosexual) Singaporeans with getting married and having children. What’s not to like?

Everything sounds great on paper. Yet, through years of research and lengthy interviews with close to a hundred parents, sociologist Teo You Yenn uncovers a different reality: “Everyday life is hectic and tense; life is stable but not quite secure; there is a pathway to follow but it does not always seem right; family is everything but family life feels off-kilter.” There is, she observes, a “sense of unease” that sits in the hearts of families in Singapore, regardless of their socioeconomic background.

title: Letter from the mudflats Hai-Dang Phan
content:
Mud envelopes my feet, dark and cool, slick with sea. It’s low tide, and the sea has receded to reveal a massive mudflat stretching as far as the eye can see. We are at Tân Thành beach, roughly two hours by car from Saigon, on the coast of Vietnam’s Mekong Delta. It is early January—the dry season in the tropical south—when huge numbers of migratory shorebirds can be found on this expanse.

Following the lead of our guide, Ba and I cautiously navigate the ankle-deep water of a tidal channel. From atop the sea wall a storm-grey heron watches our slow progress. To the north and east, fishing huts perch high on bamboo posts. To the south, giant steel transmission towers dominate the horizon as they march offshore towards rows of wind turbines. On the muddy backshore, fishing boats lie stranded with nowhere to go, outsized eyes painted on their fading prows. They are the same kind of boats that my family used when we fled the country over forty years ago.

We are sloshing across the mudflats this morning because somewhere out there might be a spoon-billed sandpiper, one of the world’s rarest shorebirds and a critically endangered species. A few regular, if elusive, birds are recorded every winter here at Tân Thành. Our guide is Bùi Thành Trung—or, as he prefers it, Toby. title: The way of the sword Simon Rowe
content:
A samurai with a katana . Credit: Nymphalyda Musashi: The Novel (Books One to Three) Eiji Yoshikawa, translated by Alexander Bennett Tuttle Publishing: 2026 . On a frigid January morning, I boarded a train from the samurai castle town of Himeji and journeyed west into the mountainous hinterland of Okayama Prefecture. Changing to a one-carriage diesel locomotive at the small town of Sayo, I continued on through long tunnels and deep valleys until, at a lonely siding, the train stopped. The sole passenger, I disembarked at the village of Miyamoto.

“Miyamoto Village lay silent,” writes Eiji Yoshikawa in the early pages of Musashi: The Novel, his sprawling samurai epic about the wandering swordsman, Miyamoto Musashi, whose search for life’s meaning takes him through the deep valleys, castle towns, and snow-bounded hinterlands of western Japan. Miyamoto Village did indeed lie silent as I trudged towards it—its traditional homesteads all but submerged in fresh snow, wooden shrines and temples groaning under the weight of the drifts.

Readers needn’t travel so far for a taste of rural Japanese antiquity. title: Philippines: the dramedy Sol Iglesias
content:
Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. Credit: Juergen Nowak / Shutterstock.com Beyond Geopolitics: The Philippines in the New Marcos Era Edited by Cleo Anne A. Calimbahim and Björn Dressel ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute: 2026 . When I need to explain the collapse of the ‘UniTeam’ alliance between President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr and his vice-president, Sara Duterte, I like to use a—ahem—highly sophisticated political paradigm of ‘Team Kadiliman (Darkness) versus Team Kasamaan (Evil)’. The reference is to a video of a hapless Harry Roque, the former Rodrigo Duterte spokesperson and current fugitive, rallying his former boss’s supporters outside Congress. In the clip, he says, in Filipino, that the battle is no longer between the Dutertes and the Marcoses. Instead, he goes, “it’s a fight between the forces of darkness versus the forces of…?” He pauses expectantly.

“Evil!” the crowd shouts innocently.

“The forces of good!” he corrects them.

To my delight, Carmel V. Abao references the same viral video in her chapter, ‘The Marcos Jr. Administration: From Populism to Reformism?’, in , edited by Cleo Anne A. Calimbahin and Björn Dressel.
